questions.question: Which of the following is considered to be a mutagen?
questions.answer: A mutagen is an agent that causes mutations. Ultraviolet light is electromagnetic radiation that damages DNA (e.g. forms thymine dimers).

questions.question: If 27% of a DNA sequence was found to be thymine, what percentage is cytosine?
questions.answer: Thymine pairs with adenine, so A = T = 27%. This leaves $100 - 54 = 46\%$ for G + C, so cytosine is $46 \div 2 = 23\%$.

questions.question: Cells of the immune system that are involved in both cell-mediated immunity and the humoral response are:
questions.answer: T helper cells activate cytotoxic T cells (cell-mediated) and B cells (humoral). Cytotoxic T cells are only involved in cell-mediated immunity.

questions.question: Sir Robert Bakewell was one of the first people in Europe to apply scientific principles to agriculture. He developed the New Leicester sheep from the old Lincolnshire sheep, by separating animals with high-quality fleece and a good fatty shoulder that was popular at the time, from the rest of the flock. This is an example of:
questions.answer: Humans chose animals with desired traits to breed: selective (artificial) breeding.

questions.question: Which of the following is a correct role of the lymph system in the immune response?
questions.answer: Lymph nodes hold lymphocytes, including memory cells, which hold the 'record' of previous infections.
options: Triggering cell death around the pathogen
Preventing entry of pathogen into the body
Holding a record of previous infection by pathogens

questions.question: Which of the processes below could cause an allele to be randomly lost from a population?
questions.answer: Genetic drift is the random change in allele frequencies, which can eliminate alleles, especially in small populations.

questions.question:
A park ranger was injected with an antivenom serum to treat a snakebite. The treating doctor explained that the injection would not protect him against future snakebites.

This is because antivenom serum is used to achieve
questions.answer: The antibodies are made elsewhere and injected, so the ranger's own immune system makes no memory cells (passive), and the exposure was deliberate (induced/artificial).

questions.question:
The steps of the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) are listed below:

I. Anneal the primers at a low temperature
II. Heat the sample to separate the DNA strands
III. Amplify the sample through many rounds
IV. Extend the sample using DNA polymerase

The correct order of steps is:
questions.answer: Denature (heat to separate strands, II), anneal primers at a lower temperature (I), extend with DNA polymerase (IV), then repeat for many cycles to amplify (III).

questions.question:
Which of the following correctly identifies male and female reproductive tissues and gametes in flowering plants?

| | Female reproductive tissue | Female gamete | Male reproductive tissue | Male gamete |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (A) | Stamen | Ovary | Stigma | Anther |
| (B) | Stigma | Ovum | Style | Pollen |
| (C) | Stigma | Ovum | Stamen | Pollen |
| (D) | Stamen | Ovary | Style | Anther |
questions.answer: The stigma (with style and ovary) is female tissue and its gamete is the ovum; the stamen is male tissue and its gamete is in the pollen.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) molecules?
questions.answer: MHC molecules are cell-surface markers that display antigens; MHC-II is found on antigen-presenting cells (and MHC-I on all nucleated cells).
options: Are found only on B and T cells

questions.question: Which of the following statements about proteins is correct?
questions.answer: Function depends on 3D shape, so changing the tertiary structure can change function. Denaturing alters the 2$^\circ$-4$^\circ$ structure but not the amino acid sequence, and some proteins are made of several polypeptides.
options: Each gene codes for a complete protein
Altering the tertiary structure can affect function
Denaturing a protein will alter its primary structure
Proteins with a quaternary structure are more biologically active than those without

questions.question:
Consider the diagram of clonal selection in B cells.

In adaptive immunity, which part of this process allows long-term (sometimes lifetime) protection against pathogens?
questions.answer: Memory cells persist for years and respond rapidly on re-exposure; plasma cells and antibodies are short-lived.
options: Recognition of one antigen by one B cell clone

questions.question:
The diagram represents the results of a gel electrophoresis.

Gel electrophoresis separates DNA, RNA or proteins based upon:
questions.answer: Fragments move through the gel at different rates depending on size: smaller molecules travel further.

questions.question:
An experiment was carried out by students to test the effect of temperature on the growth of bacteria. Bacterial cells were spread onto plates of nutrient agar that were then kept at three different temperatures: $-10$ °C, 15 °C and 25 °C. All other variables were kept constant. The experiment was carried out over four days. The nutrient agar was observed every day at the same time and the percentage of nutrient agar covered by bacteria was recorded. The results are shown in the table.

Which one of the following hypotheses is supported by the results?
questions.answer: Growth was faster at 25 °C than at 15 °C, and none at $-10$ °C. Light was not tested, temperature is the independent variable (not a result of growth) and 100% coverage was not shown.
options: If the temperature increases, then the bacteria will grow more quickly
If the bacteria are kept in the dark, then the bacteria will grow more slowly
If the bacteria grow faster, then the temperature of the location will increase
If the bacteria grow for four days, then the nutrient agar will be completely covered in bacteria

questions.question:
An experiment was carried out by students to test the effect of temperature on the growth of bacteria. Bacterial cells were spread onto plates of nutrient agar that were then kept at three different temperatures: $-10$ °C, 15 °C and 25 °C. All other variables were kept constant. The experiment was carried out over four days. The nutrient agar was observed every day at the same time and the percentage of nutrient agar covered by bacteria was recorded. The results are shown in the table.

In this experiment, the independent variable is
questions.answer: Temperature is the factor the students changed. Coverage is the dependent variable.
options: The percentage of nutrient agar covered by bacteria

questions.question:
One technique used in genetic profiling is the analysis of short tandem repeats (STRs). STRs can be used to determine the relationship between individuals. The STR profiles for six individuals are given in the table below. Individuals 1-3 are female, individuals 4-5 are male.

| STR | Individual 1 | Individual 2 | Individual 3 | Individual 4 | Individual 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| D3S1565 | 9, 13 | 5, 13 | 5, 9 | 9, 14 | 5, 9 |
| D14S617 | 12, 14 | 9, 11 | 10, 12 | 10, 14 | 10, 12 |
| D18S858 | 6, 10 | 7, 11 | 6, 8 | 7, 14 | 8, 10 |
| GATA168F06 | 25, 28 | 22, 24 | 24, 25 | 23, 28 | 22, 24 |
| ATA7D07 | 16, 18 | 15, 16 | 16, 17 | 15, 17 | 15, 17 |

Which of the following conclusions can be reached based on these data?
questions.answer: A child receives one allele at each STR from each parent. Individual 3 has one allele from Individual 1 and the other from Individual 5 at every STR (e.g. 9 from 1 and 5 from 5; 12 from 1 and 10 from 5; 6 from 1 and 8 from 5; 25 from 1 and 24 from 5; 16 from 1 and 17 from 5).
options: Individual 2 and Individual 4 could be siblings
Individual 4 could be the father of Individual 5
The parents of Individual 1 could be Individual 2 and Individual 3
Individual 3 could be the child of Individual 1 and Individual 5

questions.question:
Consider the graph of an immune response to a specific antigen introduced at point A (number of antigens, antibodies and B cells present over time).

The type of immunity shown in the diagram is
questions.answer: The body makes its own antibodies and B cells (active) after natural exposure to an antigen (natural), and this adaptive response is the third line of defence.
options: Artificial passive immunity involving the first line of defence
Natural active immunity involving the third line of defence
Natural passive immunity involving the third line of defence
Artificial active immunity involving the second line of defence

questions.question:
Consider the graph of an immune response to a specific antigen introduced at point A (number of antigens, antibodies and B cells present over time).

Which type of cell would also be expected to be increasing after point A?
questions.answer: Antibody numbers rise because B cells differentiate into plasma cells, which secrete antibodies. Helper T cells bind antigen presented on MHC (not free antigen), and dendritic cells are not stimulated by antibodies.
options: Plasma cells as they secrete antibodies to neutralise the antigen
Helper T lymphocytes that bind to the antigen
Dendritic cells that are stimulated by the production of antibodies
Cytotoxic T cells as they secrete cytokines that reduce the numbers of antigens present

questions.question:
The graph shows the HIV RNA count in the blood and the effect of the virus on the number of specific immune cells in an untreated patient.

Based on your knowledge and the information in the graph, what is the effect of the change in the number of T cells over time?
questions.answer: HIV destroys helper T cells, which coordinate the adaptive response, so as T cell numbers fall the adaptive immune system loses effective function (and viral RNA rises in the AIDS phase).
options: Failure of macrophages to engulf HIV
Loss of effective function of the adaptive immune system
A decrease in the viral RNA count during the AIDS phase

questions.question:
Modern genetic techniques have allowed scientists to determine that modern human genomes contain genetic material from the extinct *Homo* species the Neanderthals and the Denisovans. The graph shows the relative amount of Neanderthal and Denisovan DNA markers found in modern populations from around the world. Admixture of the genome indicates interbreeding between modern humans and the extinct *Homo* species.

From these data, it is reasonable to assume that:
questions.answer: Africans have very little Neanderthal admixture while all other populations have more, consistent with Neanderthals having migrated out of Africa to Europe before modern humans evolved there and spread. Some small admixture is shown in Africa, so D is not supported.
options: Modern Africans are the direct descendants of Denisovans
Modern humans evolved in Africa after Neanderthal migration to Europe
There was no interbreeding between *Homo sapiens* and either the Neanderthals or Denisovans in Africa

questions.question:
Some organisms reproduce sexually, others asexually.

Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of asexual reproduction.
questions.answer: **Advantage:** there is no need to find or attract a mate (so it is fast and energy-efficient, and a population can build up rapidly). **Disadvantage:** offspring are genetically identical, so there is little genetic diversity in the population, and the whole population is vulnerable to a single disease or environmental change.

questions.question: Compare the structure and location of DNA in prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
questions.answer: In eukaryotes the DNA is in **linear chromosomes** (wound around histones) inside a membrane-bound **nucleus**. In prokaryotes the DNA is a **circular** chromosome located in a region of the cell called the **nucleoid** (no nucleus). Prokaryotes may also have extrachromosomal DNA in plasmids, whereas eukaryotes have mtDNA in mitochondria (and cpDNA in chloroplasts).

questions.question: Construct a table to compare and contrast the features of meiosis and mitosis.
questions.answer:
| Feature | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | growth, repair, asexual reproduction | production of gametes |
| Where | body (somatic) cells | gonads (germline cells) |
| Number of divisions | one | two |
| Number of daughter cells | two | four |
| Ploidy of daughter cells | diploid ($2n$) | haploid ($n$) |
| Genetic make-up of daughter cells | identical to the parent cell | genetically different (crossing over, independent assortment) |
| Crossing over | does not occur | occurs in prophase I |

questions.question:
Describe the role of the following in gene cloning:

Ligase, plasmid, restriction enzyme, vector
questions.answer:
- **Restriction enzyme:** cuts the DNA at a specific recognition sequence, to cut out the target gene and to open the plasmid, leaving complementary sticky ends.
- **Plasmid:** a small circular piece of bacterial DNA into which the target gene is inserted; it replicates in the host so the gene is copied.
- **Ligase:** joins the target gene to the plasmid by bonding the sugar-phosphate backbones (sealing the gaps) to form recombinant DNA.
- **Vector:** carries the recombinant DNA (gene) into the host cell (e.g. a plasmid or virus), where it is replicated and expressed.

questions.question:
Human blood-calcium concentrations are under homeostatic control. When the concentration of calcium in the blood begins to fall the parathyroid gland releases parathyroid hormone. This hormone stimulates bone cells called osteoclasts to break down bone and release calcium into the blood. When the concentration of calcium rises in the blood, specialised cells associated with the thyroid gland release the hormone calcitonin. Calcitonin acts on bone and increases the amount of calcium that is deposited into bone. This information can be presented in a flowchart such as that in the figure. Note that some parts of the flowchart have been completed.

Use the information given above to complete the flowchart by filling in the six empty boxes.
questions.answer:
Left (calcium falls): **parathyroid gland** $\to$ release $\to$ **parathyroid hormone** $\to$ acts on $\to$ **bone cells called osteoclasts** $\to$ causing $\to$ **breakdown of bone and releasing calcium into the blood** $\to$ increase in blood calcium.

Right (calcium rises): cells in thyroid $\to$ release $\to$ calcitonin $\to$ acts on $\to$ **bone** $\to$ results in $\to$ **increases amount of calcium deposited into bone** $\to$ decrease in blood calcium.

questions.question:
Although plants have no immune systems, they do have many chemical and physical methods of defence against microbial pathogens and attacks by insects.

Identify one example of a physical method of defence in a plant and explain how it protects the plant.
questions.answer: A **waxy cuticle** on the leaves creates a barrier that traps or blocks pathogens, so they cannot enter the plant. (Also: thick bark is a barrier to pathogens; formation of galls limits the spread of pathogens.)

questions.question:
White clover (*Trifolium repens*) reproduces asexually from a runner that grows along the soil surface. The connected new plants are called ramets. The white clover plant in the diagram is producing ramets in the direction left to right. The fully grown ramets are numbered 1 to 7, from the youngest ramet to the oldest ramet.

Scientists hypothesised that when white clover ramets are damaged by caterpillars of *Spodoptera exigua*, the damaged ramets stimulate other ramets to defend themselves against attack by the caterpillars. The experiment used two genetically identical runners, A and B. In Stage 1, ramets 6 and 7 of Runner A were enclosed in a cage for four days; ramets 6 and 7 of Runner B were each caged with a caterpillar that was left on for four days (30% of leaf surfaces were eaten). In Stage 2, ramets 1 and 5 were cut off each runner and placed in a Petri dish, a caterpillar was released between the two ramets and allowed to feed freely, and after two days the leaf surface area eaten on each ramet was measured.

What is the role of Runner A?
questions.answer: Runner A is the **control**: it is treated the same way but without caterpillar damage, so the effect of the independent variable (earlier damage by caterpillars) can be compared.

questions.question:
White clover (*Trifolium repens*) reproduces asexually from a runner that grows along the soil surface. The connected new plants are called ramets. The white clover plant in the diagram is producing ramets in the direction left to right. The fully grown ramets are numbered 1 to 7, from the youngest ramet to the oldest ramet.

Scientists hypothesised that when white clover ramets are damaged by caterpillars of *Spodoptera exigua*, the damaged ramets stimulate other ramets to defend themselves against attack by the caterpillars. The experiment used two genetically identical runners, A and B. In Stage 1, ramets 6 and 7 of Runner A were enclosed in a cage for four days; ramets 6 and 7 of Runner B were each caged with a caterpillar that was left on for four days (30% of leaf surfaces were eaten). In Stage 2, ramets 1 and 5 were cut off each runner and placed in a Petri dish, a caterpillar was released between the two ramets and allowed to feed freely, and after two days the leaf surface area eaten on each ramet was measured.

The experiment was repeated 40 times. The average results obtained after Stage 2 are shown in the graph.

Referring to the data, compare the average leaf surface area of young ramets eaten by the caterpillar in Runner A and Runner B.
questions.answer: An average of about **0.6 cm$^2$** of young ramet leaf was eaten in Runner A, compared with about **0.15 cm$^2$** in Runner B: approximately four times as much young leaf area was eaten in Runner A.

questions.question:
White clover (*Trifolium repens*) reproduces asexually from a runner that grows along the soil surface. The connected new plants are called ramets. The white clover plant in the diagram is producing ramets in the direction left to right. The fully grown ramets are numbered 1 to 7, from the youngest ramet to the oldest ramet.

Scientists hypothesised that when white clover ramets are damaged by caterpillars of *Spodoptera exigua*, the damaged ramets stimulate other ramets to defend themselves against attack by the caterpillars. The experiment used two genetically identical runners, A and B. In Stage 1, ramets 6 and 7 of Runner A were enclosed in a cage for four days; ramets 6 and 7 of Runner B were each caged with a caterpillar that was left on for four days (30% of leaf surfaces were eaten). In Stage 2, ramets 1 and 5 were cut off each runner and placed in a Petri dish, a caterpillar was released between the two ramets and allowed to feed freely, and after two days the leaf surface area eaten on each ramet was measured.

After the experiments, the contents of the leaves were analysed. Significantly higher quantities of phenolic acid were found in the young ramets from Runner B. Phenolic acid acts as a signalling molecule that can act as an agent in plant defence to protect the plant from future attack. It was noticed that the caterpillars preferred to eat the mature leaves in Runner B.

Suggest an effect of the signalling molecule on cells of the young leaves that would account for the caterpillars' preference for eating the mature leaves in Runner B.
questions.answer: The phenolic acid in the young leaf cells may make them **less tasty or less digestible** (or toxic) to the caterpillars, so the caterpillars are selectively repelled from the young leaves and feed on the mature leaves instead.

questions.question: Assess the effect of cell replication processes on the genetic code and the continuity of a species.
questions.answer:
**Maintaining the genetic code:** before mitosis and meiosis, DNA is replicated semi-conservatively using complementary base pairing, so each daughter cell receives an exact copy of the genetic code. Mitosis produces genetically identical cells, which maintains the code for growth and repair, and for asexual reproduction.

**Variation:** meiosis produces gametes with half the chromosomes. Crossing over (swapping segments between homologous chromosomes in prophase I) and independent assortment of chromosomes produce new combinations of alleles, and random fertilisation adds more variation. Occasional errors in replication (mutations) add new alleles.

**Assessment for continuity:** accurate copying preserves successful genetic information from one generation to the next, while meiosis gives the genetic variation on which natural selection acts, so some individuals survive environmental change and reproduce. Together they ensure the continuity of the species, although asexual reproduction by mitosis alone leaves a population vulnerable because it lacks variation.

questions.question:
The graphs show different information about the effectiveness of antibiotics as a treatment strategy for infectious disease (deaths from infectious disease 1930-2000, and the increase in antibiotic resistance 1999-2008).

Using the information provided in the graphs and your knowledge, discuss the effectiveness of antibiotics as a treatment strategy for infectious diseases.
questions.answer:
Antibiotics kill bacteria (or stop them reproducing), so they treat bacterial infections. The first graph shows deaths from infectious disease fell from about 200 per 100 000 people in 1930 to about 25 by about 1955, after penicillin was first used in 1942, so antibiotics were very effective (although hygiene and vaccination also contributed). The rate has stayed at about 25-50 since then, with a slight rise in the 1980s-90s.

The second graph shows the percentage of bacteria resistant to antibiotics rising between 1999 and 2008 (e.g. ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin from about 4% to a peak of about 22% in 2006, other antibiotics from about 1-3% to about 5-8%). Overuse leads to natural selection of resistant bacteria, so antibiotics are becoming less effective. Overall, antibiotics have been highly effective, but resistance threatens their future effectiveness, and they do not work on viruses.

questions.question:
The pedigree for a particular trait is shown. The allele for the trait is dominant.

Explain why the trait is not sex-linked.
questions.answer:
- **Not Y-linked:** females (individuals 3 and 11) have the trait, but they do not have a Y chromosome.
- **Not X-linked dominant:** an affected male passes his X chromosome (with the dominant allele) to all his daughters, so all daughters would be affected. Individual 4 has the trait but his daughter, individual 9, does not.
- (X-linked recessive is excluded because the allele is dominant.)

So the trait must be autosomal dominant.

questions.question:
The pedigree for a particular trait is shown. The allele for the trait is dominant.

Identify the genotype of Individual 1. Give a reason for your answer.
questions.answer: **Aa** (heterozygous). He has the trait, so he has at least one dominant allele $A$. His children 5 and 6 do not have the trait ($aa$), and each must have received an $a$ allele from him (as their mother, individual 2, is $aa$).

questions.question:
The pedigree for a particular trait is shown. The allele for the trait is dominant.

If Individuals 7 and 8 were to have another child, what is the likelihood of the child possessing the trait? Use a Punnett square to illustrate your answer.
questions.answer:
Individual 7 has the trait; his mother (5) is $aa$, so he is **Aa**. Individual 8 does not have the trait: **aa**.

| | $a$ | $a$ |
|---|---|---|
| $A$ | $Aa$ | $Aa$ |
| $a$ | $aa$ | $aa$ |

Probability of a child with the trait = $\frac{2}{4} = \mathbf{50\%}$.

questions.question: Scientists have used biotechnology to create herbicide resistant strains of canola. Explain one advantage of using biotechnology in place of artificial pollination, and explain the potential impact of biotechnology in farming on genetic diversity.
questions.answer:
**Advantage:** biotechnology can introduce a specific desired gene (e.g. herbicide resistance) directly into the crop in one generation, whereas artificial pollination relies on cross-breeding and takes many generations of selection (and unwanted traits are transferred along with the desired one). It is therefore faster and more precise, and can transfer genes between species.

**Impact on genetic diversity:** if farmers grow only a few genetically modified (identical) strains, genetic diversity in crops decreases, and traditional varieties could be lost, so the crop is more vulnerable to a new disease or pest or to environmental change. Transgenes can also spread to wild relatives, and herbicide-resistant weeds could develop.

questions.question:
A student investigated the effectiveness of hand washing. They recruited thirty students who then deliberately contaminated their hands with hard surfaces such as hand rails, desks and door knobs in the classrooms. The students were then randomly assigned to one of three groups: (1) no hand washing, (2) hand washing with tap water or (3) hand washing with soap and tap water. Instructions were given as to how to wash their hands and for what length of time. Swabs were then taken from the volunteers' hands and transferred to agar plates. The plates were incubated at 30 °C for 48 hours. The percentage coverage of two types of bacteria that are found in the intestines of animals was calculated and recorded in the table.

| Hand washing technique | Percent of sample with *Enterococcus* spp. bacteria (%) | Percent of sample with *Enterobacter amnigenus* bacteria (%) |
|---|---|---|
| No hand washing | 30 | 12 |
| Water | 15 | 3 |
| Water and soap | 5 | 3 |

Draw an appropriate graph of the results.
questions.answer: A **column graph** with handwashing technique on the x-axis, percentage of sample with bacteria (%) on the y-axis (scale 0-35), two different shaded columns for each technique (*Enterococcus* and *Enterobacter*), plotted correctly and with a key.

questions.question:
A student investigated the effectiveness of hand washing. They recruited thirty students who then deliberately contaminated their hands with hard surfaces such as hand rails, desks and door knobs in the classrooms. The students were then randomly assigned to one of three groups: (1) no hand washing, (2) hand washing with tap water or (3) hand washing with soap and tap water. Instructions were given as to how to wash their hands and for what length of time. Swabs were then taken from the volunteers' hands and transferred to agar plates. The plates were incubated at 30 °C for 48 hours. The percentage coverage of two types of bacteria that are found in the intestines of animals was calculated and recorded in the table.

| Hand washing technique | Percent of sample with *Enterococcus* spp. bacteria (%) | Percent of sample with *Enterobacter amnigenus* bacteria (%) |
|---|---|---|
| No hand washing | 30 | 12 |
| Water | 15 | 3 |
| Water and soap | 5 | 3 |

Explain the results in the graph.
questions.answer:
Washing reduced bacterial growth for both bacteria, and **soap and water was the most effective**. *Enterococcus* fell from 30% (no washing) to 15% with water and 5% with soap and water (an 83% reduction). Soap lowers the surface tension and breaks down the oily film/membranes, lifting bacteria off the skin so they are rinsed away.

For *Enterobacter amnigenus* the reduction was from 12% to 3% with water alone, and there was no further reduction with soap (3%), so water alone was as effective as soap for this bacterium, which suggests that rinsing is the key step for it (it is more easily removed).

questions.question:
Protein synthesis includes the processes of transcription and translation.

Describe the steps in transcription.
questions.answer: Transcription occurs in the nucleus. The enzyme **helicase** unwinds and unzips a section of the DNA (a gene), and one strand acts as the template. **RNA polymerase** moves along the template strand and joins free RNA nucleotides by complementary base pairing (A-U, T-A, C-G, G-C) to form a strand of **mRNA**. The mRNA detaches and leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore, and the DNA re-forms its double helix.

questions.question:
Protein synthesis includes the processes of transcription and translation.

Assess the significance of a mutation in a non-coding section of DNA.
questions.answer: Non-coding DNA does not code for amino acids, so a mutation there usually has **no effect on the protein or the phenotype**, so it is often neutral and not significant. However, some non-coding sequences have functions (e.g. promoters, regulatory sequences, introns containing splice sites), so a mutation in them can change gene expression or how the mRNA is spliced and so affect the phenotype. Mutations in non-coding DNA are also useful as markers for tracing ancestry, and can accumulate over generations. Overall, most such mutations have little effect, but some can be significant.

questions.question:
The diagram represents a part of protein synthesis (a ribosome on an mRNA strand, with tRNAs bringing amino acids to form a polypeptide; the structures X and Y are labelled).

Identify the structures labelled X and Y in the diagram, and the location in which the process takes place.
questions.answer: **X:** tRNA (transfer RNA). **Y:** ribosome. **Location:** the cytoplasm (translation).

questions.question:
The diagram represents a part of protein synthesis (a ribosome on an mRNA strand, with tRNAs bringing amino acids to form a polypeptide; the structures X and Y are labelled).

Describe the purpose of mRNA in this process.
questions.answer: mRNA carries the genetic code (a copy of the gene) from the DNA in the nucleus to the ribosome in the cytoplasm. The sequence of its codons determines the order of the amino acids brought by tRNA, and so the sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide.

questions.question:
Zika fever is a rapidly emerging viral disease. It is most commonly transferred from one person to another through the bite of an infected *Aedes* mosquito but can also be transferred from an infected pregnant woman to her foetus, through sexual activity and blood transfusions.

Zika fever in people was first discovered in Uganda in 1947. It was thought that a bite from a mosquito had transferred the virus from monkeys to humans. Since then, it has spread slowly across the globe, with outbreaks most recently in the Americas in 2015 and 2016.

The symptoms of Zika fever are usually mild, ranging from rash, headache, joint and muscle pain to fever. Approximately 80% of infected humans do not show symptoms. Infection of pregnant women, however, can cause severe defects in their babies.

When scientists attempt to identify a particular disease, they can look for specific antibodies in infected humans. Scientists trying to identify Zika infections found that testing for the antibodies produced against the Zika virus often gave them incorrect results. This was because the antibody tests that had been developed could not always identify the difference between the antibodies produced against the Zika virus and the antibodies produced against other viruses.

The graph shows the number of Zika virus cases across the regions of Brazil during 2016.

Describe the trend shown in the graph.
questions.answer: The graph shows the number of Zika cases in each of five Brazilian regions in 2016. Cases rose rapidly to a peak at about week 8-10 (more than 8000 cases in the Northeast region, the highest, with the Southeast and North lower) and then fell significantly after about week 20, to very low numbers by about week 30 onwards.

questions.question:
Zika fever is a rapidly emerging viral disease. It is most commonly transferred from one person to another through the bite of an infected *Aedes* mosquito but can also be transferred from an infected pregnant woman to her foetus, through sexual activity and blood transfusions.

Zika fever in people was first discovered in Uganda in 1947. It was thought that a bite from a mosquito had transferred the virus from monkeys to humans. Since then, it has spread slowly across the globe, with outbreaks most recently in the Americas in 2015 and 2016.

The symptoms of Zika fever are usually mild, ranging from rash, headache, joint and muscle pain to fever. Approximately 80% of infected humans do not show symptoms. Infection of pregnant women, however, can cause severe defects in their babies.

When scientists attempt to identify a particular disease, they can look for specific antibodies in infected humans. Scientists trying to identify Zika infections found that testing for the antibodies produced against the Zika virus often gave them incorrect results. This was because the antibody tests that had been developed could not always identify the difference between the antibodies produced against the Zika virus and the antibodies produced against other viruses.

The graph shows the number of Zika virus cases across the regions of Brazil during 2016.

Explain how Koch's postulates can be used to establish a causal relationship between a microbe and a disease and identify ONE reason why it may not be possible to apply these postulates to the Zika virus.
questions.answer:
1. The microorganism must be found in all diseased individuals but not in healthy individuals.
2. The microorganism must be isolated from the diseased individual and grown in pure culture.
3. Inoculating a healthy host with the cultured microorganism must cause the same disease.
4. The microorganism must be re-isolated from the inoculated, diseased host and shown to be the same as the original.

**Limitation:** viruses cannot be grown in pure culture on agar (they need living host cells). Also, about 80% of people infected with Zika show no symptoms, so the microbe is found in people without disease (postulate 1), and it would be unethical to infect healthy humans.

questions.question:
Zika fever is a rapidly emerging viral disease. It is most commonly transferred from one person to another through the bite of an infected *Aedes* mosquito but can also be transferred from an infected pregnant woman to her foetus, through sexual activity and blood transfusions.

Zika fever in people was first discovered in Uganda in 1947. It was thought that a bite from a mosquito had transferred the virus from monkeys to humans. Since then, it has spread slowly across the globe, with outbreaks most recently in the Americas in 2015 and 2016.

The symptoms of Zika fever are usually mild, ranging from rash, headache, joint and muscle pain to fever. Approximately 80% of infected humans do not show symptoms. Infection of pregnant women, however, can cause severe defects in their babies.

When scientists attempt to identify a particular disease, they can look for specific antibodies in infected humans. Scientists trying to identify Zika infections found that testing for the antibodies produced against the Zika virus often gave them incorrect results. This was because the antibody tests that had been developed could not always identify the difference between the antibodies produced against the Zika virus and the antibodies produced against other viruses.

The graph shows the number of Zika virus cases across the regions of Brazil during 2016.

Provide an explanation as to why the antibody tests could not identify the difference between the antibodies produced against the Zika virus and the antibodies produced against other viruses.
questions.answer: Antibodies are specific to the shape of an antigen. The antigens on the Zika virus and on related viruses have a **similar shape**, so the same antibody can bind to the antigen-binding site of both, and the test cannot tell them apart.

questions.question:
The graph shows the level of antibodies found in the blood after first and second exposure to an antigen such as the Zika virus.

Compare the first exposure to the second exposure in terms of changes to antibody concentration.
questions.answer:
- First exposure: antibodies start to be produced about 7 days after exposure; second exposure: antibodies start to be produced within a few days (a faster response).
- First exposure: the peak is reached at about day 18 and is low (a small peak); second exposure: the peak is reached sooner (about 10 days after exposure) and is much **higher**.
- First exposure: antibody levels fall to near zero after the peak; second exposure: levels stay high for a longer period.

questions.question: Explain why the combined use of public health campaigns and vaccination is a more effective way of controlling disease than using only one of these strategies. Support your answer using examples.
questions.answer:
**Vaccination** gives immunity to individuals without them having the disease: it stimulates the adaptive immune system to make memory cells. When enough of the population is immune (herd immunity), the spread of the pathogen is reduced. Example: the HPV vaccine prevents infection with the viruses that cause cervical cancer, and the MMR vaccine protects against measles. But vaccination does not work for every disease, can take time to develop, needs high uptake, and takes time to work (e.g. for COVID-19 in 2020).

**Public health campaigns** educate people and change behaviour to reduce transmission, e.g. hand washing, social distancing, masks, safe sex campaigns, mosquito-control and quarantine measures, and they also promote vaccination uptake. Example: the 'Slip, Slop, Slap' campaign reduced skin cancer; and during COVID-19 mask wearing and distancing slowed the spread. But they rely on people changing their behaviour and do not give immunity to those who are exposed.

**Combined:** campaigns raise awareness of the disease and the benefits and safety of vaccines, so vaccination rates are higher (e.g. COVID-19 vaccination campaigns), and they reduce transmission while vaccine coverage builds up or for diseases without a vaccine. Vaccination then protects people who do not or cannot follow the advice. The two together give both individual immunity and reduced exposure, so they control disease more effectively than either alone (e.g. polio and measles control relies on vaccination programs supported by public education and surveillance).
